Patient Vignette: Marcus R.

Marcus sits in the chair with his back perfectly straight, his hands resting flat on his thighs. He is a tax consultant, thirty-six years old, married for eight years to a woman named Elena. He tells me that he chose tax work because it is predictable. Numbers do not lie, he says. They do not change. They follow rules.

He was a different man twelve years ago. He was a squad leader in an infantry unit, deployed to a provincial capital in the Middle East. His job was to clear buildings. He tells me about the morning of October 14th, 2012, with the same flat, measured tone he uses to describe a client's audit history. His squad had been tasked with entering a compound near a market. Intelligence had been wrong before, but this time it was catastrophically wrong. The building was rigged. He was the second man through the door when the blast threw him backward into the street. He landed on his back, ears ringing, dust and smoke so thick he could not see his own hands. He remembers the sound. Not the explosion itself, but the high, thin whine that followed, and then the screaming. His medic, a kid named Perez, had been directly in front of him. There was not enough of Perez left to carry.

Marcus does not talk about the rest of that day. He says he does not remember it, and I believe him. He remembers waking up in a field hospital three days later with a concussion and a perforated eardrum. He was sent home six weeks after that. Medically evacuated. He tells me he was fine for the first year. He got the job at the firm. He married Elena. He thought he had escaped.

The change came slowly. He started noticing it about four years ago. He would be sitting at his desk, reviewing a client's 1099 forms, and the sound of a car backfiring on the street would send him under his desk. He would stay there, heart hammering, waiting for the second blast. His assistant found him once. He told her he dropped a pen. He does not think she believed him.

Now, he cannot go to the grocery store. The aisles are too narrow, and he cannot see the exits. He has to check every room in his house before he can sit down. He has to sit with his back to the wall in restaurants. He stopped going to restaurants two years ago. Elena eats out with her friends now. He stays home.

He dreams about Perez. Not the explosion, but the moments before it. In the dream, he always has time to stop. He always has time to pull Perez back. He always wakes up reaching for something that is not there. He wakes up sweating, his fists clenched, and he cannot get back to sleep. He gets up and goes to his home office. He works. He says the numbers are the only thing that quiet the noise.

He is irritable. He knows this. He snaps at Elena when she asks him simple questions. He told her last week that she was trying to trap him, that she was testing him, and he saw the hurt in her face and he did not know how to take it back. He does not feel like himself. He feels like a wire that is pulled too tight, waiting to snap. He told me that he is tired. Not sleepy, he clarified. Tired. Bone-tired. The kind of tired that comes from being afraid all the time, for years, for no reason he can explain.

He looks at me with steady eyes. He is not crying. He is not shaking. He is telling me these things the way he would tell me about a quarterly loss. He is a man who has learned to report his own suffering as data. But his hands are still flat on his thighs, and they are perfectly still.
